body.text: Picture the daypack by the door: water, a snack, a notebook, a charged phone and a plan for Saturday. Most towns already have the rest, whether that's a trail, a big park, a river path or a market, and a few small things in the bag make each one nicer.

This list gives you fifteen outings, each with the one piece of gear worth bringing and a prompt for finding your own version. It uses kinds of places rather than named ones, so it works wherever you live. Entry fees and rules vary by place, so check before you go.

items: **Water and a snack.** A daypack or bag makes it easy to carry both, plus a spare layer.
**A bag that carries it all.** Hands free beats hands full.
**A small notebook.** For finds, names of birds and the café you want to come back to.
**A charged phone.** For the map, the time and a photo or two.

body.text: **Before you leave:** check opening times and local rules, since a closed gate is the quickest way to flatten an adventure. Go with someone when you can, and tell someone your plan, especially somewhere remote or after dark. Stick to well-lit areas, check the weather and daylight, and trust your instincts; no plan removes every risk.

body.title: A nature trail you've never walked
body.note: Search your area for a short, marked trail under two hours, and wear comfortable shoes. Go with a friend, tell someone your route, check the weather and carry water. **What makes it easier:** walking shoes with grip, trekking-style socks and a small daypack, so your feet are comfortable and water and a layer ride on your back.

body.title: The big park on the far side of town
body.note: Not your nearest one; the one you always mean to visit. Take a ball, a blanket and a book. **What makes it easier:** a picnic blanket and a daypack, so a ball, a book and a snack travel together and there's always a dry place to sit.

body.title: A river or lakeside path
body.note: Water makes any walk feel like a small trip. Walk to the first bench, sit, then carry on. **What makes it easier:** a phone armband, so a playlist or a map is there without a hand on your phone.

body.title: A sunrise or sunset spot
body.note: Find a high point or an open field. Check local times and bring a layer. **Worth bringing:** an insulated flask of something warm, so the wait for the light is cozy.

body.title: A bike or bus ride to the end of the line
body.note: Choose a route, get off at the last stop and have a look around. Bring a map or a charged phone. If you would rather ride, [how to get into recreational cycling as an adult](/journal/how-to-get-into-recreational-cycling-as-an-adult) starts from a borrowed bike. **What makes it easier:** a compact daypack, so a snack, water and a layer stay on your back at the last stop.

body.title: For your first trail morning
body.dek: Walking shoes, socks made for walking, a daypack, a bottle and a phone armband turn "let's go for a walk" into a plan you can leave the house for.

body.title: A morning of birdwatching
body.note: A pond, wetland or quiet corner of a park. Bring a notebook and a bird-ID app or a field guide. **Worth bringing:** compact binoculars and a pocket notebook, which bring a distant branch close enough to see the colors and give each sighting a line.

body.title: A sketching afternoon in public
body.note: Take a pencil and a small sketchbook somewhere with a view and draw what's in front of you for an hour. Fancy adding color? [Watercolor painting for beginners](/journal/watercolor-painting-for-beginners) shows how small the setup can be. **What makes it easier:** a pocket-size sketch pad and a black fineliner ({{product:sakura-pigma-micron-8-pack-black|a pack of black fineliner pens}} is one option), so outlines go down quickly on a bench.

body.title: A stargazing night
body.note: Find a dark spot away from streetlights, bring a blanket and a flask, and check the forecast for clear skies. Go with a friend or tell someone where you'll be. **What makes it easier:** a picnic blanket you can lie back on, so the ground is comfortable while you look up.

body.title: A photo walk through an old quarter
body.note: Walk it like a visitor. Read the plaques, look above the shopfronts, take a few photographs. **Nice to have:** a reusable film camera, so each frame is one you chose rather than one you snapped.

body.title: For slower, closer looking
body.dek: Binoculars, a pocket notebook, a sketch pad, a travel watercolor set or a film camera give a quiet hour something to do and something to bring home.

body.title: A farmers' or flea market
body.note: Go early. Bring a tote, a little cash and a plan to taste something new. **What makes it easier:** a roomy market tote, so produce and finds ride on your shoulder and your hands stay free.

body.title: A thrift-store crawl
body.note: Visit three in an afternoon with a small budget. Look for one thing you'd never buy new. **Worth bringing:** a sturdy tote for the finds, plus comfortable walking shoes for the walk between shops.

body.title: A picnic or potluck in the park
body.note: Everyone brings one dish. A feast on a tiny budget, with logistics that mostly look after themselves. **What makes it easier:** a picnic blanket and an insulated cooler bag, so everyone's dish has a place to sit and the spread looks like a spread.

body.title: A secondhand bookshop
body.note: Head for a section you never visit and buy one book on instinct. **Worth bringing:** a book sleeve, so the book you pick on instinct gets home with its cover intact.

body.title: A group walk with tea
body.note: Ask a few friends to meet at a trailhead or park. Finish with tea or a shared snack. **What makes it easier:** an insulated flask, so there's tea at the halfway bench for everyone to share.

body.title: A day as a tourist in your own city
body.note: Build a mini itinerary: morning walk, lunch, a gallery, an evening view. Do it with a visitor's curiosity. **What makes it easier:** comfortable walking shoes and a small daypack, so a morning walk, lunch, a gallery and an evening view fit into one day.

body.title: For market and picnic days
body.dek: A blanket, a flask, a tote and an insulated bag carry the day, so the spread, the finds and the tea all arrive in one piece.

body.text: Some of the nicest outings need no ticket at all. Check entry fees, hours and parking before you go; many places have free days or free hours.

items: A library branch you've never entered: some have gardens, exhibitions or beautiful reading rooms. Borrow something unexpected.
A museum on a free or discounted day, or a free gallery or community art space. Choose the piece you'd take home.
A botanical or public garden, many of which have free or low-cost days.
A community event or open day, a volunteering shift or a free or pay-what-you-can class. Check notice boards, library bulletins and neighborhood groups, and contact organizers first.
A quiet public building: many places of worship and historic halls welcome visitors for a look around. Follow local etiquette and dress codes.
A neighborhood you never go to, or a scavenger hunt of your own: write ten things to spot around town and see who reaches ten first.

body.text: Pick one category from this list and search your area for a nearby match. Check opening times, entry costs and any rules, pack water, a snack and one small thing to do there, and put it in your calendar with a start time.

For a fuller list, see [things to do on the weekend](/journal/things-to-do-on-the-weekend), or stay in with an [at-home creative weekend](/journal/at-home-creative-weekend). Curious about a new hobby? See [15 hobbies to start this month](/journal/affordable-hobbies-under-25).
